tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. * `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.

# Intent Brief — Aviation Maintenance Handbook Assistant

**Client / sponsor:** An aircraft maintenance operations organization (assumed; simulated case).
**Primary end user:** The person running maintenance operations for aircraft (stated).
**Current job-to-be-done:** Answering maintenance questions by searching the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician General Handbook.
**Core pain:** Questions are nested and their answers span several chapters, so a single search misses parts (stated).
**Desired outcome:** A chat assistant whose answers capture everything the handbook says, with citations (stated).
**One demonstrable user journey:** Ask a multi-part question → get a cited answer from every relevant chapter → run a corpus-wide check that confirms nothing relevant was missed.
**Candidate must-haves (max 3):**
1. Metadata-rich ingestion of the Markdown chapters — the main focus (stated).
2. Fast, cited answers to nested, multi-chapter questions (stated).
3. A corpus-wide completeness check (stated).
**Explicit non-goals:** Figures/images, aircraft-specific manuals, access control, exam mode, deployment, local models (inferred / stated).
**Data and access reality:** Only the 14 Markdown chapter bodies may be used. The table of contents, book index, glossary and PDF navigation data are prohibited (stated). The OpenRouter key works (observed).
**Critical constraints:** 60-minute build; hosted inference through OpenRouter only; pickle storage, no database; every topic supported by Markdown text (all stated). Safety-critical domain; keys only through environment variables.
**Success signal:** Multi-chapter answers cite every relevant section. Measured as recall against ground truth from an LLM reading the full chapters, spot-checked by the user (inferred).
**Unacceptable failure:** Stating something the handbook does not support, or silently leaving out a relevant chapter (assumed).
**Decision record:**
- Confirmed by stakeholder: user, pain, recall priority, fast-plus-verify approach, 60 minutes, ingestion focus, OpenRouter with OpenAI models, Markdown-only corpus, pickle storage.
- Observed / supplied: 14 chapter files with page markers; working key.
- Assumed by FDE: unacceptable failure, non-goals, glossary excluded, LLM-judged recall.
- Unresolved / defer to real client: acceptable answer latency.
**Handoff to architect:** Scope the smallest working MVP against the desired outcome; establish API contract, ≥3 acceptance criteria, ≥2 failure modes, and assign independent workstreams.

1	# MASTER SPEC — Aviation Maintenance Handbook Assistant (v1)
2	> State: **FROZEN v1** — approved by the user on 2026-11-01 and committed on `main`. The baseline SHA is recorded in the dispatch handoff (it is not embedded here).
3	> Authoritative: this document controls the three task briefs. After freeze, `specs/*` and `docs/INTENT_BRIEF.md` are read-only by team policy.
4	> Revision 2 (user decisions): all AI inference is hosted through OpenRouter; OpenAI models; the corpus is the Markdown chapter bodies only; storage is pickle files plus in-memory search.
5	
6	## Global client contract
7	- **Client problem / end user / outcome:** The person running aircraft maintenance operations asks nested questions whose answers span several chapters of the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician General Handbook. They need a chat assistant whose answers capture everything the handbook says, with citations (see `docs/INTENT_BRIEF.md`).
8	- **Corpus (strict):** only the 14 Markdown chapter bodies, `corpus/ch01_*.md` … `corpus/ch14_*.md`. Documents are discovered by filename pattern; the chapter number and title come from the Markdown H1.
9	- **Prohibited inputs** for routing, embeddings, metadata or evaluation:
10	  - `corpus/00_front-matter.md` (table of contents)
11	  - `corpus/index.md` (book index)
12	  - `corpus/glossary.md`
13	  - `corpus/manifest.json`
14	  - PDF bookmarks or outlines, and anything under `DATA/`
15	- **Page markers:** the `<!-- page 13-1 (pdf p.616) -->` markers inside the Markdown are used **only** to label citations. They are stripped from all text that gets embedded, BM25-indexed or sent to an LLM.
16	- **Demo slice:** user asks a multi-part question → fast cited answer from every relevant chapter → user switches on **Verify** → coverage report lists any relevant section the fast answer missed.
17	- **Three MVP must-haves:**
18	  1. **Metadata-rich index** (main focus): document → section → chunk hierarchy built from Markdown headings; LLM document profiles, section cards and chunk enrichment; topics backed by verified quotes and normalized into one topic list; stored in pickle files.
19	  2. **Fast mode** `ask()`: intent, sub-questions, hybrid dense + BM25 search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), API-based relevance assessment, context expansion, an answer citing every contributing section.
20	  3. **Verify mode:** a sweep over all section metadata that reports relevant sections missing from the fast answer.
21	- **Non-goals:**

Output: a two-level topic list (`topic_id`, `label`, `parent_id`) and a mapping from each raw label to a canonical topic. Every canonical topic must come from at least one grounded raw topic.

126	   - dense top 40 chunks, plus dense top 10 sections expanded to their chunks;
127	   - BM25 top 40;

160	def verify_coverage(question: str, intent: dict, citations: list[dict],
161	                    store: dict) -> dict  # Coverage
162	```

## Global client contract
- **Client problem / end user / outcome:** The person running aircraft maintenance operations asks nested questions whose answers span several chapters of the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician General Handbook. # entity    = {"text": str, "type": <entity enum>, "evidence_quote": str}
- **IDs:** section `ch07.s012`, chunk `ch07.s012.c02`. A `doc_id` is the corpus file stem.
- **`content_type` enum:** procedure | concept | regulation | table | safety | calculation | definition | other
- **Entity `type` enum:** component | material | tool | process | regulation | part_number | specification | condition | safety_hazard | other
- **`enrichment.source`:** `"llm"` or `"failed"`. A section whose LLM step failed keeps its text, chunks and vectors, but has an empty summary and empty topics.

```python
class IndexReport(BaseModel):
    documents: int; sections: int; chunks: int; pages_covered: int; pages_expected: int
    sections_enriched: int; sections_failed: int
    topics_raw: int; topics_dropped_unsupported: int; taxonomy_size: int
    llm_calls: int; llm_cost_usd: float; embedding_inputs: int
    embedding_model: str; llm_model: str; built_at: str; failures: list[str]
```

Loader for everyone: `rag.store.load_store(path="index/store.pkl") -> dict`. It checks `schema_version` and the embedding model, and builds the in-memory BM25 index once.

### B. `rag.ask` — owned by Claude, called by the UI
```python
def ask(question: str, history: list[dict] | None = None,
        mode: Literal["fast", "verify"] = "fast") -> dict  # Answer, JSON-serialisable
```
**Pipeline:**
1. Validate the input.
2. **Intent call** (`LLM_MODEL`). This also rewrites a follow-up so it stands alone, using the last 6 turns. Output: `{primary, intents[], topics[topic_id], entities[], sub_questions[], keyword_query, needs_clarification}`.
3. **Search, for each sub-question:**
   - dense top 40 chunks, plus dense top 10 sections expanded to their chunks;
   - BM25 top 40;
   - merge with RRF (k=60);
   - apply a soft topic boost. Topics never filter results out.
   - Keep the top 30 candidates.
4. **Relevance assessment** (`LLM_MODEL`, one call per sub-question, sub-questions in parallel). Each candidate gets a score from 0 to 3 with a reason. Keep scores of 2 or more, at most 8 per sub-question.
5. **Context expansion.** Add the chunks on either side within the same section, or the whole section if it is under about 1,500 tokens. Total budget is about 12k tokens.
6. **Answer** (`ANSWER_MODEL`, structured JSON). It uses only the supplied passages, puts a `[n]` marker on every claim, and sets `insufficient_evidence` when the passages don't support an answer.
7. **Verify mode only:** `rag.verify.verify_coverage`.

**Answer shape** (see `specs/fixtures/answer_fast.json` and `answer_verify.json`):

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `answer_markdown` | str | Inline `[n]` markers |
| `citations` | list | `{n, section_id, doc_id, chapter, section_path, page_label, snippet, relevance}`; `relevance` is 0–3 from step 4 |
| `intent` | obj | `{primary, intents[], topics[], entities[{text,type}], needs_clarification: str\|null}` |
| `sub_questions` | list | `{question, citation_ns[]}` |
| `coverage` | obj\|null | `null` in fast mode; `Coverage` in verify mode |
| `insufficient_evidence` | bool | |
| `mode` | str | `"fast"` or `"verify"` |
| `latency_ms` | int | |
| `error` | obj\|null | `{code, message}` |

- **`intent.primary` enum:** fact_lookup | definition | how_to | troubleshooting | comparison | calculation | regulatory | navigation | multi_hop | out_of_scope
- **`error.code` enum:** `empty_question`, `question_too_long` (over 2,000 characters), `index_missing`, `provider_unavailable`, `timeout`
- **Never raises.** Errors come back in `error`.
- **Timeouts:** fast mode 60 s overall. Verify mode adds at most 45 s. Each provider call gets 30 s and 2 retries.
- **Degraded mode:**
  - If the LLM is unavailable but embeddings work, return the top passages from dense + BM25 + RRF as the answer, with `error.code = provider_unavailable`.
  - If embeddings are unavailable, use BM25 only.

### C. `rag.verify.verify_coverage` — owned by Codex, called by `ask` in verify mode
```python
def verify_coverage(question: str, intent: dict, citations: list[dict],
                    store: dict) -> dict  # Coverage
```
**Coverage:**
```json
{"chapters_cited": [8, 9], "chapters_relevant": [2, 8, 9],
 "missed_sections": [{"section_id": "...", "section_path": "...", "page_label": "...", "reason": "..."}],
 "complete": false}
```
- Sweeps **every** section in `store["sections"]` using its topics, entities, keywords, questions, summary and section vector.
- Takes the uncited candidates (top 20) and asks `LLM_MODEL` to judge relevance.
- Must finish within the verify timeout.
- Hosted inference only.

### Mock fixtures
- `specs/fixtures/answer_fast.json`
- `specs/fixtures/answer_verify.json`
- `specs/fixtures/section_record.json`
- `specs/fixtures/chunk_record.json`

These are labeled MOCK; their content is illustrative, not verified handbook output.

## Acceptance criteria and failure handling
1. **Index coverage and grounding.** Given the 14 chapter files, when `python -m ingest.build` runs, then `report.json` shows:
   - all 14 documents and every chapter page covered;
   - every chunk inside exactly one section;
   - every kept `evidence_quote` and entity text found verbatim, after normalization, in its source Markdown;
   - every canonical topic traceable to at least one grounded raw topic;
   - a vector shape of (N, 1536) for chunks and sections.
2. **No prohibited inputs, no local inference.** Given the built store, then:
   - every `doc_id` matches `ch\d\d_*`;
   - ingestion never opens `00_front-matter.md`, `index.md`, `glossary.md`, `manifest.json` or `DATA/`;
   - no repo code imports `chromadb`, `onnxruntime`, `fastembed`, `sentence_transformers` or `torch`.
3. **Multi-chapter answer.** Given a nested question whose ground truth spans two or more chapters, when `ask(mode="fast")` runs, then the citations include sections from those chapters, as measured by criterion 5.
4. **Verify flags misses.** Given a question where a relevant section is not cited, when `ask(mode="verify")` runs, then `coverage.missed_sections` lists it with a page label and `complete` is false. When nothing is missed, `complete` is true.
5. **Measured recall.** Given `evals/golden.jsonl`, when `python -m evals.recall` runs, then it prints section-level and chapter-level Recall@k for fast and verify modes.
   - The golden set has 15 or more nested questions, written by hand or generated from chapter text.
   - Ground truth comes from `LLM_MODEL` reading the full chapter bodies (sections marked) and marking the relevant `section_id`s with verified quotes.
   - The user spot-checks at least 5 questions.
   - Actual numbers are reported; no target is invented.
   - No index, table of contents or glossary is used.

**Failure cases:**
- **Not covered by the handbook** (e.g. "torque for a Cessna 172 main wheel axle nut"): `insufficient_evidence` is true and no value is invented.
- **OpenRouter error or rate limit during ingestion:** the build continues; failed sections are marked `"failed"`; re-running replays `llm_cache.pkl` and `embed_cache.pkl` and calls only what is missing.
- **Ungrounded LLM output:** topics or entities whose quotes aren't found in the source are dropped and counted. They never reach the store.
- **Empty or over-long question:** the matching `error.code` is returned; the UI shows it without crashing.

**First smoke test:** run `python -m ingest.build --only ch13`. Expect `report.json` to show 1 document and 8 pages, with grounding counts. Then `ask("What may a mechanic with an airframe rating approve for return to service?")` should return citations with page labels 13-x.

**Evidence to record:** command output, the `report.json` summary, demo Q&A, recall table, commit SHAs.

## CLAUDE OWNERSHIP
- **Worktree:** `C:/Users/amber/code/fde-coding-challenge`, branch `main`.
- **Owns:** `ingest/`, `rag/` (except `rag/verify.py`), `index/` (generated), `scripts/`, `requirements.txt`, `README.md`, and integration.
- **First artifact (~15 min):** `ingest.build --only ch13` writes `store.pkl`, the two cache files and `report.json` with grounded LLM enrichment. Commit and announce the SHA.
- **Handoff:** full store committed, then `rag.ask` working in fast mode.

## CURSOR OWNERSHIP
- **Worktree:** `C:/Users/amber/code/fde-coding-challenge/.worktrees/cursor-isolated-work`, branch `cursor/isolated-work`.
- **Owns:** `ui/` only.
- **Builds:** a Gradio chat app (`python -m ui.app`) with a Fast/Verify toggle, a citations panel with relevance, a coverage panel, and visible sub-questions. Uses `rag.ask` when importable; `MOCK=1` uses the fixtures instead.
- **States:** idle, loading, error, success, insufficient evidence.
- **First artifact (~15 min):** a mock UI rendering both fixtures.
- **Handoff:** commit SHA and a screenshot.

## CODEX OWNERSHIP (ACTIVE)
- **Worktree:** `C:/Users/amber/.codex/worktrees/fde-challenge-work/fde-coding-challenge`, branch `codex/fde-challenge-work`.
- **Owns:** `rag/verify.py`, `evals/`, `tests/`.
- **Builds:**
  - `verify_coverage` per contract C;
  - contract tests for the fixtures and the `store.pkl` schema;
  - the prohibited-input and no-local-inference tests (criterion 2);
  - `evals/golden.jsonl` with LLM-judged ground truth (criterion 5);
  - `python -m evals.recall`.
- **First artifact (~15 min):** contract tests plus `verify_coverage` running against a small `store`-shaped dict built from the fixtures.
- **Activation:** yes. The user chose three workers.

## Integration / release protocol
- **Baseline SHA:** recorded in the dispatch handoff after the freeze commit. The existing worktrees are at `f1c96c4` and must merge `main` at the baseline.
- **Worktree locations:** confirmed with `git worktree list`.
- **Checkpoints:** about 15 minutes after dispatch, and again at about 30 minutes. Claude integrates and reviews.
- **Spec changes:** go through `docs/decisions/CHANGE_REQUEST.md`, need user approval, and are applied as v2.
- **Priority:** a working local app first. The Gradio share link is optional; Render is out of scope.
- **Feature freeze:** about 10 minutes before the end. After that, evaluation and demo only.

1	# Intent Brief — Aviation Maintenance Handbook Assistant
2	
3	**Client / sponsor:** An aircraft maintenance operations organization (assumed; simulated case).
4	**Primary end user:** The person running maintenance operations for aircraft (stated).
5	**Current job-to-be-done:** Answering maintenance questions by searching the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician General Handbook.
6	**Core pain:** Questions are nested and their answers span several chapters, so a single search misses parts (stated).
7	**Desired outcome:** A chat assistant whose answers capture everything the handbook says, with citations (stated).
8	**One demonstrable user journey:** Ask a multi-part question → get a cited answer from every relevant chapter → run a corpus-wide check that confirms nothing relevant was missed.
9	**Candidate must-haves (max 3):**
10	1. Metadata-rich ingestion of the Markdown chapters — the main focus (stated).
11	2. Fast, cited answers to nested, multi-chapter questions (stated).
12	3. A corpus-wide completeness check (stated).
13	**Explicit non-goals:** Figures/images, aircraft-specific manuals, access control, exam mode, deployment, local models (inferred / stated).
14	**Data and access reality:** Only the 14 Markdown chapter bodies may be used. The table of contents, book index, glossary and PDF navigation data are prohibited (stated). The OpenRouter key works (observed).
15	**Critical constraints:** 60-minute build; hosted inference through OpenRouter only; pickle storage, no database; every topic supported by Markdown text (all stated). Safety-critical domain; keys only through environment variables.
16	**Success signal:** Multi-chapter answers cite every relevant section. Measured as recall against ground truth from an LLM reading the full chapters, spot-checked by the user (inferred).
17	**Unacceptable failure:** Stating something the handbook does not support, or silently leaving out a relevant chapter (assumed).
18	**Decision record:**
19	- Confirmed by stakeholder: user, pain, recall priority, fast-plus-verify approach, 60 minutes, ingestion focus, OpenRouter with OpenAI models, Markdown-only corpus, pickle storage.
20	- Observed / supplied: 14 chapter files with page markers; working key.
21	- Assumed by FDE: unacceptable failure, non-goals, glossary excluded, LLM-judged recall.
22	- Unresolved / defer to real client: acceptable answer latency.
23	**Handoff to architect:** Scope the smallest working MVP against the desired outcome; establish API contract, ≥3 acceptance criteria, ≥2 failure modes, and assign independent workstreams.
24

1	# MASTER SPEC — Aviation Maintenance Handbook Assistant (v1)
2	> State: **FROZEN v1** — approved by the user on 2026-11-01 and committed on `main`. The baseline SHA is recorded in the dispatch handoff (it is not embedded here).
3	> Authoritative: this document controls the three task briefs. After freeze, `specs/*` and `docs/INTENT_BRIEF.md` are read-only by team policy.
4	> Revision 2 (user decisions): all AI inference is hosted through OpenRouter; OpenAI models; the corpus is the Markdown chapter bodies only; storage is pickle files plus in-memory search.
5	
6	## Global client contract
7	- **Client problem / end user / outcome:** The person running aircraft maintenance operations asks nested questions whose answers span several chapters of the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician General Handbook. They need a chat assistant whose answers capture everything the handbook says, with citations (see `docs/INTENT_BRIEF.md`).
8	- **Corpus (strict):** only the 14 Markdown chapter bodies, `corpus/ch01_*.md` … `corpus/ch14_*.md`. Documents are discovered by filename pattern; the chapter number and title come from the Markdown H1.
9	- **Prohibited inputs** for routing, embeddings, metadata or evaluation:
10	  - `corpus/00_front-matter.md` (table of contents)
11	  - `corpus/index.md` (book index)
12	  - `corpus/glossary.md`
13	  - `corpus/manifest.json`
14	  - PDF bookmarks or outlines, and anything under `DATA/`
15	- **Page markers:** the `<!-- page 13-1 (pdf p.616) -->` markers inside the Markdown are used **only** to label citations. They are stripped from all text that gets embedded, BM25-indexed or sent to an LLM.
16	- **Demo slice:** user asks a multi-part question → fast cited answer from every relevant chapter → user switches on **Verify** → coverage report lists any relevant section the fast answer missed.
17	- **Three MVP must-haves:**
18	  1. **Metadata-rich index** (main focus): document → section → chunk hierarchy built from Markdown headings; LLM document profiles, section cards and chunk enrichment; topics backed by verified quotes and normalized into one topic list; stored in pickle files.
19	  2. **Fast mode** `ask()`: intent, sub-questions, hybrid dense + BM25 search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), API-based relevance assessment, context expansion, an answer citing every contributing section.
20	  3. **Verify mode:** a sweep over all section metadata that reports relevant sections missing from the fast answer.
21	- **Non-goals:**
22	  - any local model inference (BGE, FastEmbed, ONNX, sentence-transformers, local cross-encoders, ChromaDB's built-in embedder);
23	  - a vector database or other database;
24	  - figures/images, aircraft-specific manuals, access control, exam mode, long-term memory, Render deployment.
25	- **Facts vs assumptions:**
26	  - Stated by user: end user, multi-chapter pain, recall as the priority, fast-plus-verify approach, 60-minute budget, OpenRouter, the models, Markdown-only corpus, pickle storage, every section enriched, verify as a metadata sweep, three workers.
27	  - Assumed: unacceptable failure, non-goals, excluding the glossary (strict reading of "chapter bodies"), and the LLM-judged evaluation ground truth.
28	- **Security / privacy / cost:**
29	  - `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` lives only in `.env`, which is gitignored. It never appears in the UI, logs, fixtures or pickle files.
30	  - **Pickle rule:** load only pickle files produced by this repo's pipeline. Never load user-supplied pickles, because unpickling can execute code.
31	  - The content is public.
32	  - Estimated ingestion cost is about $4–5, using `gpt-4.1-mini` with about 1,460 calls. The Markdown has 1,441 styled headings.
33	
34	### Models (all through OpenRouter, `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`, `Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY`)
35	
36	| Role | Env var | Default | Verified |
37	|---|---|---|---|
38	| Embeddings, both ingestion and query | `EMBEDDING_MODEL` | `openai/text-embedding-3-small` (1536-d) via `POST /embeddings` | live call OK, 1536-d |
39	| Profiling, topic extraction, topic-list normalization, chunk enrichment, intent, relevance assessment, verify judge | `LLM_MODEL` | `openai/gpt-4.1-mini` via `POST /chat/completions` with `response_format: json_schema` (strict) | live call OK |
40	| Grounded final answer | `ANSWER_MODEL` | `openai/gpt-4.1` | live call OK |
41	
42	The same embedding model must be used for ingestion and queries. The query path refuses to run (`index_missing`) if `store.pkl` was built with a different `EMBEDDING_MODEL`.
43	
44	### Architecture
45	- One Python process: Gradio UI → `rag.ask()` → OpenRouter.
46	- Search is fully in memory: NumPy cosine similarity over L2-normalized float32 vectors, plus `rank-bm25` rebuilt from stored tokens at load.
47	- **Rejected alternatives:**
48	  - ChromaDB or another vector database: no time to set it up, and Chroma's default embedder is local inference.
49	  - Sending the whole book to the model on every question: slow and costly per query.
50	
51	### Ingestion pipeline (Claude): every LLM step is structured JSON, cached, and resumable
52	1. **Parse.** Read the 14 chapter files and record page markers for citations.
53	   - Build sections from **Markdown heading lines only**. The H1 is the chapter. Heading style decides the level: bold headings are sections, bold-italic headings are subsections.
54	   - Section IDs follow document order.
55	2. **Chunk.** Split within sections at paragraph boundaries, aiming for 300–500 tokens. A chunk never crosses a section boundary. Tables, numbered steps and warnings stay whole.
56	3. **E1 Document profile** (14 calls). Input: the full chapter body. Output: summary, scope, raw topics with evidence quotes, key entities.
57	4. **E2 Section and chunk enrichment** (about 1,440 calls, one per section, 16 at a time; a section under about 150 tokens is merged into the one before it). Input: the document profile summary plus the section text with chunk boundaries marked. Output:
58	   - section summary, `content_type`, raw topics `{label, evidence_quote}`, entities `{text, type, evidence_quote}`, keywords, questions answered;
59	   - for each chunk: `{chunk_id, context_line, topics[]}`. The context line is one or two sentences placing the chunk within its section.
60	5. **Grounding check** (in code, not an LLM). Every `evidence_quote` and entity `text` must appear in its source Markdown after normalization (case, whitespace and Markdown emphasis ignored).
61	   - On failure: retry once, asking for exact quotes. If it still fails, drop the item.
62	   - Dropped counts go into the report.
63	   - Reason: in testing, `gpt-4.1-mini` returned non-verbatim "quotes".
64	6. **E3 Topic-list normalization** (one or a few calls). Input: the grounded raw topic labels with counts. Output: a two-level topic list (`topic_id`, `label`, `parent_id`) and a mapping from each raw label to a canonical topic. Every canonical topic must come from at least one grounded raw topic.
65	7. **Apply topics** in code: map canonical `topic_id`s onto documents, sections and chunks.
66	8. **Embed** in batches of up to 128 inputs:
67	   - chunk text = `section_path + "\n" + context_line + "\n\n" + chunk_text`, with page markers stripped;
68	   - section text = `summary + questions`;
69	   - document text = profile summary.
70	9. **BM25 tokens** cover the chunk text plus the section's keywords and entity texts.
71	10. **Write** the pickle files and `report.json`.
72

74	Contract type: **Python functions** (single-process Gradio app; no HTTP service).

117	### B. `rag.ask` — owned by Claude, called by the UI
118	```python
119	def ask(question: str, history: list[dict] | None = None,
120	        mode: Literal["fast", "verify"] = "fast") -> dict  # Answer, JSON-serialisable
121	```
122	**Pipeline:**
123	1. Validate the input.
124	2. **Intent call** (`LLM_MODEL`). This also rewrites a follow-up so it stands alone, using the last 6 turns. Output: `{primary, intents[], topics[topic_id], entities[], sub_questions[], keyword_query, needs_clarification}`.
125	3. **Search, for each sub-question:**
126	   - dense top 40 chunks, plus dense top 10 sections expanded to their chunks;
127	   - BM25 top 40;
128	   - merge with RRF (k=60);
129	   - apply a soft topic boost. Topics never filter results out.
130	   - Keep the top 30 candidates.
131	4. **Relevance assessment** (`LLM_MODEL`, one call per sub-question, sub-questions in parallel). Each candidate gets a score from 0 to 3 with a reason. Keep scores of 2 or more, at most 8 per sub-question.
132	5. **Context expansion.** Add the chunks on either side within the same section, or the whole section if it is under about 1,500 tokens. Total budget is about 12k tokens.
133	6. **Answer** (`ANSWER_MODEL`, structured JSON). It uses only the supplied passages, puts a `[n]` marker on every claim, and sets `insufficient_evidence` when the passages don't support an answer.
134	7. **Verify mode only:** `rag.verify.verify_coverage`.
135	
136	**Answer shape** (see `specs/fixtures/answer_fast.json` and `answer_verify.json`):
137	
138	| Field | Type | Notes |
139	|---|---|---|
140	| `answer_markdown` | str | Inline `[n]` markers |
141	| `citations` | list | `{n, section_id, doc_id, chapter, section_path, page_label, snippet, relevance}`; `relevance` is 0–3 from step 4 |
142	| `intent` | obj | `{primary, intents[], topics[], entities[{text,type}], needs_clarification: str\|null}` |
143	| `sub_questions` | list | `{question, citation_ns[]}` |
144	| `coverage` | obj\|null | `null` in fast mode; `Coverage` in verify mode |
145	| `insufficient_evidence` | bool | |
146	| `mode` | str | `"fast"` or `"verify"` |
147	| `latency_ms` | int | |
148	| `error` | obj\|null | `{code, message}` |
149	
150	- **`intent.primary` enum:** fact_lookup | definition | how_to | troubleshooting | comparison | calculation | regulatory | navigation | multi_hop | out_of_scope
151	- **`error.code` enum:** `empty_question`, `question_too_long` (over 2,000 characters), `index_missing`, `provider_unavailable`, `timeout`
152	- **Never raises.** Errors come back in `error`.
153	- **Timeouts:** fast mode 60 s overall. Verify mode adds at most 45 s. Each provider call gets 30 s and 2 retries.
154	- **Degraded mode:**
155	  - If the LLM is unavailable but embeddings work, return the top passages from dense + BM25 + RRF as the answer, with `error.code = provider_unavailable`.
156	  - If embeddings are unavailable, use BM25 only.

158	### C. `rag.verify.verify_coverage` — owned by Codex, called by `ask` in verify mode
159	```python
160	def verify_coverage(question: str, intent: dict, citations: list[dict],
161	                    store: dict) -> dict  # Coverage
162	```
163	**Coverage:**
164	```json
165	{"chapters_cited": [8, 9], "chapters_relevant": [2, 8, 9],
166	 "missed_sections": [{"section_id": "...", "section_path": "...", "page_label": "...", "reason": "..."}],
167	 "complete": false}
168	```
169	- Sweeps **every** section in `store["sections"]` using its topics, entities, keywords, questions, summary and section vector.
170	- Takes the uncited candidates (top 20) and asks `LLM_MODEL` to judge relevance.
171	- Must finish within the verify timeout.
172	- Hosted inference only.

182	## Acceptance criteria and failure handling
183	1. **Index coverage and grounding.** Given the 14 chapter files, when `python -m ingest.build` runs, then `report.json` shows:
184	   - all 14 documents and every chapter page covered;
185	   - every chunk inside exactly one section;
186	   - every kept `evidence_quote` and entity text found verbatim, after normalization, in its source Markdown;
187	   - every canonical topic traceable to at least one grounded raw topic;
188	   - a vector shape of (N, 1536) for chunks and sections.
189	2. **No prohibited inputs, no local inference.** Given the built store, then:
190	   - every `doc_id` matches `ch\d\d_*`;
191	   - ingestion never opens `00_front-matter.md`, `index.md`, `glossary.md`, `manifest.json` or `DATA/`;
192	   - no repo code imports `chromadb`, `onnxruntime`, `fastembed`, `sentence_transformers` or `torch`.
193	3. **Multi-chapter answer.** Given a nested question whose ground truth spans two or more chapters, when `ask(mode="fast")` runs, then the citations include sections from those chapters, as measured by criterion 5.
194	4. **Verify flags misses.** Given a question where a relevant section is not cited, when `ask(mode="verify")` runs, then `coverage.missed_sections` lists it with a page label and `complete` is false. When nothing is missed, `complete` is true.
195	5. **Measured recall.** Given `evals/golden.jsonl`, when `python -m evals.recall` runs, then it prints section-level and chapter-level Recall@k for fast and verify modes.
196	   - The golden set has 15 or more nested questions, written by hand or generated from chapter text.
197	   - Ground truth comes from `LLM_MODEL` reading the full chapter bodies (sections marked) and marking the relevant `section_id`s with verified quotes.
198	   - The user spot-checks at least 5 questions.
199	   - Actual numbers are reported; no target is invented.
200	   - No index, table of contents or glossary is used.
201	
202	**Failure cases:**
203	- **Not covered by the handbook** (e.g. "torque for a Cessna 172 main wheel axle nut"): `insufficient_evidence` is true and no value is invented.
204	- **OpenRouter error or rate limit during ingestion:** the build continues; failed sections are marked `"failed"`; re-running replays `llm_cache.pkl` and `embed_cache.pkl` and calls only what is missing.
205	- **Ungrounded LLM output:** topics or entities whose quotes aren't found in the source are dropped and counted. They never reach the store.
206	- **Empty or over-long question:** the matching `error.code` is returned; the UI shows it without crashing.
207	
208	**First smoke test:** run `python -m ingest.build --only ch13`. Expect `report.json` to show 1 document and 8 pages, with grounding counts. Then `ask("What may a mechanic with an airframe rating approve for return to service?")` should return citations with page labels 13-x.

210	**Evidence to record:** command output, the `report.json` summary, demo Q&A, recall table, commit SHAs.

### 1. How do I recognize corrosion on aluminum aircraft parts?
Corrosion on aluminum surfaces is usually quite obvious. The products of corrosion are white and generally more voluminous than the original base metal. Even in its early stages, aluminum corrosion is evident as general etching, pitting, or roughness of the aluminum surfaces. On the surface of aluminum alloys, it appears as pitting and etching and is often combined with a gray or white powdery deposit. When these deposits are removed, the surface may appear etched and pitted, depending on the length of exposure and severity of attack. # One-Slide Pitch — Maintenance Handbook Assistant

**Audience:** the business owner who runs maintenance operations (non-technical).
**Source of truth:** `specs/MASTER_SPEC.md`, `docs/INTENT_BRIEF.md`, `index/report.json`, and a live run of the working assistant on 2026-11-01.
**Case note:** the demo uses the public FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician General Handbook as a stand-in for the client's own documents.

---

## The slide

**Title:** Ask a maintenance question in plain English. Get a cited answer from every chapter that matters.

| The problem today | What we built | What you see |
|---|---|---|
| Technicians ask questions that touch several chapters. A single search finds one piece and misses the rest. | A chat assistant that has read all 14 handbook chapters (633 pages). | A plain-English answer, with each statement tagged to its chapter, section and page. |

**Live example (real output, not a mock):**
> *"How do I recognize corrosion on aluminum aircraft parts, how is it treated, and what must be recorded afterward?"*
> The assistant split this into three questions and answered all three. It cited Chapter 8 (corrosion signs and treatment, pages 8-17 to 8-22) and Chapter 2 (maintenance record entries, page 2-39). That is two chapters from one question, in about 18 seconds.

**Why it makes life easier**
- One question instead of hunting through chapters.
- Every answer shows where it came from, so a technician or inspector can check the page.
- If the handbook does not cover something, the assistant says so instead of guessing.

**Completeness check ("Verify"):** after the quick answer, a second pass sweeps every section of the handbook and lists anything relevant that the answer left out. *It is built but not yet reliable; see "Not yet proven".*

**What a pilot would prove (the success measures):**
1. Do answers include every relevant section? We measure this against a question set your own experts write.
2. Do technicians spend less time finding answers than they do today?
3. Do your experts trust the citations when they spot-check them?

**Not yet proven (said out loud, not hidden):**
- We have **no measured accuracy or recall number yet**. The test set that would produce one has not been run.
- The completeness check returned an error on every test question today. It needs a fix before it is shown as working.
- Answer time was about 15–25 seconds per question. Your acceptable wait time is still an open question.

---

## 90-second talk track

**(0:00)** "Your technicians already have the answers. They are in the handbooks. The problem is that real questions don't live in one place. Ask how to deal with corrosion on an aluminum part, and the answer is in one chapter, the paperwork rule is in another, and a search finds only one of them."

**(0:20)** "So we built an assistant that has read the whole handbook, all 14 chapters and 633 pages. A technician types the question the way they would say it out loud."

**(0:35)** *Show the corrosion question.* "Watch what it does. It breaks the question into three parts: how to spot it, how to treat it, and what to record. It answers each part, and every statement has a number that links to a chapter, a section and a page. Here it pulled from Chapter 8 for the corrosion work and Chapter 2 for the record-keeping rule. One question, two chapters."

**(1:00)** "Two things matter for trust. First, nothing is unsourced: if a technician or an inspector doubts an answer, the page is right there. Second, if the handbook doesn't cover it, the assistant says so rather than inventing a number."

**(1:15)** "What we are not claiming: we haven't measured accuracy yet, and the 'did it miss anything' check isn't ready. What we'd like to do is a short pilot on your real documents, with questions your own experts write, and measure whether it finds everything and saves your people time."

**(1:30)** "That's the ask: agree on ten to fifteen real questions, and we'll show you the results."

---

## Q&A prep (20-minute live session)

| Likely question | Honest answer |
|---|---|
| How accurate is it? | Not measured yet. The pilot measures it against questions your experts write. |
| Will it miss things? | Possibly. The completeness check is meant to catch that, but it is not working reliably yet. Citations let a person check any answer. |
| Can it use our own manuals, not just the FAA handbook? | The approach is designed for that. This build covers the FAA handbook only; your documents would be a pilot step. |
| What if it's wrong? | Every claim carries a page reference, and it declines when the text doesn't support an answer. A person still makes the maintenance decision. |
| How long does it take? | About 15–25 seconds per question in today's runs. |
| What does it cost to set up and run? | Reading the 14-chapter handbook into the system cost about $3.31 in AI usage. Per-question cost has not been measured. |
| Who can see our data? | This case uses a public handbook. Handling of your private documents would be agreed before any pilot. |

---

## Evidence behind this page

| Claim on the slide | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| 14 chapters, 633 pages, all covered | `index/report.json` (documents 14, pages covered 633 of 633) |
| About $3.31 to read the handbook in | `index/report.json` (`llm_cost_usd` 3.3099) |
| Corrosion question: Ch 8 and Ch 2 cited, ~18 s | Live run of `rag.ask(mode="fast")`, 2026-11-01 |
| Completeness check errors | Live runs of `rag.ask(mode="verify")`, 3 of 3 returned `provider_unavailable` |
| No accuracy number | `evals/` does not exist yet; the recall run (acceptance criterion 5) has not been done |

## Before the live session
- Use a **real screenshot** of a fast-mode answer. `ui/screenshots/*.png` show the mock fixtures (the Verify one is partly cropped), so do not present them as real results.
- Run the corrosion question once beforehand so the demo is warm, and keep the local app as the fallback. There is no cloud URL to claim.
- Fix or hide the Verify toggle before the demo, or present it as "coming next".
